content.thinking:
I'm working out the fur colors and body details, then setting up the fork and hand geometry per side using vector math along the fork path to position joints correctly.

From there I'm computing the wrist and palm positions as capsule segments relative to the fork point, chaining the arm joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist) with the digit chain parented to the wrist tip, and sweeping the arm fur along a catmull path through the key joint points.

Now I'm working out the leg socket positions - hip, knee, ankle - checking the distances between joints to make sure the thigh and shin bulk proportions line up with the foot resting on the branch, then placing the toe origin point for the foot.

Adding points to wrap the toe around the branch, but computing arc length shows each toe would come out around 0.19m, way too long for a koala's actual ~6cm toes -- I need to shrink the radius or angle span.

For hands, I'm recalculating the grip radius against the branch at that height, then settling on a finger wrap angle around 140° to avoid oversized hands while keeping the chunky pixel style. I'll mirror the same approach for thumbs, angling them outward on the opposite side.

Now I'm laying out the hand digit offsets, spacing three fingers and two thumbs along the inner/outer axis, then planning the foot pad as a dark capsule from ankle to toe. Setting up imports for the Joint type and geometry merging utilities, then starting to write the twig scattering helper and its data type for position, direction, and length.

Still writing twig generation logic...

I'm checking whether hanging leaves near the fork twigs at z≥0.3 would overlap the koala's face region — since the face sits around y=0.8 and z≤0.19, leaves hanging to y≈0.92 stay above and clear of it, so I just need to keep twig x-positions bounded to avoid drifting in front of the face.

With roughly 20 twigs and 7 leaves each, that's around 140 leaf cards to place. Now I'm turning to stand details — plaque, mushrooms, pebbles, grass cards, fallen leaves, a ladybug, and bark patches — making sure the stump bottom sits flush at y=0.

I'm defining the torso as a swept chain shaped more like a pear, with radius keyframes that are wider at the hips and taper elsewhere, interpolated smoothly along the spine.

Now I'm adding a neck capsule connecting the chest to the head base, then fur-covered ears with darker outer and cream inner coloring, jaw tufts, a thin mouth line, and texture-based skin paints for the muzzle and face regions.

I'm also placing a small leaf card near the mouth, figuring out how its flow direction should orient the face so it reads correctly from the front rather than from above or the side.

Now I'm switching to the plaque: planning a wood plank base with a brass plate, sizing the texture plane dimensions so each pixel maps cleanly to a texel for stamping text onto it.

I'm figuring out the plaque's position and rotation on the stump top, tilting it roughly 35 degrees and computing how the base and front edge seat against the stump surface so it sinks in slightly rather than floating.

For the text plane, I'm aligning its orientation with the plaque's rotated axes so the surface normal matches the box's tilt, and I'm settling on a cream text color against a dark brown plate with a contrasting border.

Now I'm working out the moss patch near the trunk base, computing its outline relative to the stump's top position, and building the column-scanning logic that generates contiguous row spans for each column to form the moss shape.

For the gumnuts, I'm planning to merge several small spheres into a single geometry using translated instances at each gumnut position, then attach the merged shape to the appropriate bone.

I'm scattering grass card positions in a ring around the moss edge on the stump, oriented facing upward with small random sizes and crossed blades for fullness. With the root rig and plinth details sorted, I'm ready to write out the full file.
